key_facts: A record-low pharmacy count: 9,999 bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16], rising slightly to 10,526 by February 2026 but still 9% below February 2016 levels [17].

Severe staffing pressure: 60% of pharmacy teams report staffing shortages, 54% of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff, 81% of staff report longer patient waits, 57% report reduced ability to give advice [17].

A structural shift in ownership from large multiples (down from 5,220 pharmacies in 2021 to 3,283, i.e. 32.8% market share) toward small independents (up from 4,024 to 4,910, now 49%+ market share) [16].

Continued "financial crisis" framing by the sector's negotiating body, Community Pharmacy England (CPE), even after securing the 10.3% uplift, which it says will cover "growth in activity and inflation... but will not make further progress towards delivering sustainability" [5][10][14].
quantitative_anchors: Pharmacy First budget now folded into CPCF (previously separate £215m line in 2025/26; £8m digital developments also folded in) [6].
Prior year (2025/26) uplift was **19.7%** — so 2026/27's 10.3% represents a marked deceleration [5][9].
Margin allowance uplift: **£200 million** added to annual margin, taking retained margin to **£1.1 billion** [10].
Historic over-delivery write-off: **up to £239 million** (up to end of March 2026) [6][10], following a prior **£193 million** write-off agreed for 2024/25 [8].
Single Activity Fee (SAF): rose from £1.27 → £1.46 (April 2025) [8] → **£1.52** (backdated to May 2026) [9].
Pharmacy First consultation fee: rose from £15 → **£17** [4].
Banded fixed payments: **£500** for 20-29 consultations/month; **£1,000** for 30+ consultations/month [2][4][5].
Prescription charge (2026): **£9.90 per item** [3].
Independent prescribing (IP) set-up: **£500 one-off fee** + **£525/month infrastructure fee** per contractor [5].
IP expansion funding: **£340 million** government deal for autumn 2026 rollout [3][7].

Consultation volumes: **3.3 million** PF consultations March 2025–Feb 2026 (**+43% YoY**) [3][7]; **2.75 million** clinical pathway consultations April 2025–Jan 2026 [6]; **~1 million** contraception consultations and **~3 million** hypertension case-finding consultations in the same 10-month window [6]; **~1 billion** prescription items dispensed in the same period [6]; **254,692** PF consultations/month by June 2025, up from **125,275**/month in Feb 2024 [21]; **5.4 million** cumulative PF consultations Jan 2024–Feb 2025 [22]; **4.5 million** consultations claimed Feb 2024–Oct 2025 [17].

Pharmacy count: **9,999** bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16]; **10,526** as of February 2026 (down 9% / 1,083 fewer than Feb 2016's 11,609) [17]; **10,900** participating in PF as of October 2025 [17].
Closures: **274 closures** Jan 2024–March 2025 (>5/week average) [16]; **~1,000+ closures** Feb 2016–Feb 2026 [17].

Ownership shift: small independents (1-5 branches) grew from **4,024 (2021) → 4,910 (March 2025)**, now **49%+ market share**; large chains (100+) fell from **5,220 (2021) → 3,283**, now **32.8% market share**; medium groups (6-99) at **18%+ / 1,807 pharmacies** [16].

Staffing: **60%** of pharmacy teams report shortages; **54%** of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff; **81%** report longer patient waits; **57%** report reduced ability to give advice (CPE Pharmacy Pressures Survey, June 2025, n=4,300 owners/head-office reps + 1,600 team members) [17].

Band caps (March 2026 schedule): Band 1 (<18/month avg) capped at 45 paid; Band 6 (47+/month avg) capped at 234 paid [1]. By April 2026 schedule, Band 6 cap falls to just **120** [1] — a **~49% reduction** in the space of two monthly schedule updates.

Employer NI rise (Budget effective April 2025): **13.8% → 15%** on salaries above a lowered £5,000 threshold (from £9,100) [15] — NHS-exempt but pharmacy contractor status uncertain/likely non-exempt, a major cost pressure compounding cap effects.
Tax rise flagged for pharmacy business sales: **4% tax increase** from April 2026 affecting exit/succession planning [11].

## What are the costs and who is exempt?

The pharmacist consultation itself is free on the NHS. However, any medicine supplied under Pharmacy First is subject to normal NHS prescription charges. As of 2026, the standard prescription charge is £9.90 per item. This is the same charge you would pay for a medicine collected from a GP prescription.

The table below summarises who pays and who is exempt: [...] | Major expansion from autumn 2026 | A £340 million government deal enables independent pharmacist prescribing, building on 3.3 million consultations delivered in one year. | [...] The scale of existing demand makes this expansion logical. Between March 2025 and February 2026, over 3.3 million consultations were delivered under Pharmacy First in England, representing a 43% increase year on year. That figure reflects genuine patient appetite for accessible, fast, pharmacist-led care. The expansion is designed to meet that demand while simultaneously reducing pressure on GP surgeries and A&E departments.

The current capping mechanism for Pharmacy First consultations will be retained, and a similar approach will be used for IP consultations. This means there will be two caps within each band: one applicable to pharmacies signed up to provide prescribing services, and one for those who are not offering the new prescribing services.

Fixed payments will remain at £500 for contractors delivering 20 to 29 consultations in a month and £1,000 for those delivering 30 consultations or more, regardless of whether they are prescribing consultations or not.

CPE also agreed a two-month late claim window for Pharmacy First and the New Medicine Service (NMS) – the two advanced services that still have a one-month claim window – giving contractors a total of three months to make a claim. [...] The DHSC said the initial introduction of independent prescribing during 2026/27 will be funded through a one-off £500 set-up fee, payable once a contractor has signed up to deliver the relevant service, and a £525 monthly infrastructure fee.

CPE said that bacterial conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis, oral thrush, skin infections and respiratory tract infections are services that would be considered for the expanded Pharmacy First service.

During the summer, NHS England will create a clinical reference group of experts across primary care who will consider the new pathways for IPs under Pharmacy First, The Pharmacist understands. [...] ## A £340 million funding uplift

The headline funding announcement is that community pharmacy funding will rise by £340 million funding in 2026/27 after Community Pharmacy England (CPE) accepted the government’s offer.

This will see the sector’s budget increase by 10.3% to £3.636 billion – higher than the NHS overall increase of 2.7%, but significantly lower than last year’s 19.7% funding boost.

The Pharmacist understands that this is not new money but will come from the total NHS funding (£225bn) announced at the 2026/27 Spending Review.

CPE has warned that the new funding will cover growth in activity and inflation in the coming year but will not make further progress towards delivering sustainability to the sector.

# Q1 2025 Pharmacy Market Update

## Momentum Builds Despite Sector Headwinds.

The UK pharmacy market entered 2025 with a surprising surge in acquisition activity. Despite broader economic pressures – including stubborn inflation, ongoing NHS funding constraints and increasing costs as a result of the previous Labour budget – buyer demand for community pharmacies has sharply increased.

Q1 saw a noticeable uptick in average offers based on EBITDA multiples, faster transaction timelines, and renewed confidence from both multiples and independent operators.

### Buyer Activity on the Rise [...] Working in partnership with Prospect Health, one of the UKs largest healthcare recruitment specialists, Prospect Estates have unrivalled access to pharmacists looking to move in to ownership and we’re well placed to keep you in tune with first-time buyer trends and patterns.

Q1 2025 Pharmacy Market Update

### Sector Challenges and the New Pharmacy Contract

This uptick comes amid real challenges. The UK pharmacy sector continues to navigate staffing challenges, rising costs, and increased clinical service expectations under the new 2025/26 Community Pharmacy Contractual Framework (CPCF). While the contract brings welcome clarity and modest funding increases for clinical services, many pharmacy owners are still under pressure to do more with less. [...] However, this very environment is also prompting a wave of consolidation. Some owners are choosing to exit while valuations are holding, while buyers are banking on long-term upside as the role of community pharmacy in primary care expands.

### Our verdict

The outlook for the pharmacy market for the remainder of 2025 looks positive so far – you can follow our blog posts for regular updates and perceived changes.

We urge anyone considering their short and mid-term exit strategy to be mindful of the 4% tax increases coming in April 2026. Whilst the speed of pharmacy transaction has increased, it’s advisable for owners to plan their timelines, and get their ducks in a row, well in advance of a sale becoming a reality.

# Large multiples: feeling the financial squeeze

How the UK’s four largest community pharmacy chains are coping with the current financial climate and the strategies they are employing to tackle the challenges it brings.

Large pharmacy crosses

Julie Lee / The Pharmaceutical Journal

Great Britain’s big pharmacy chains may be able to leverage economies of scale but they are not immune to the financial climate affecting the sector, with the four largest — Boots, LloydsPharmacy, Well Pharmacy and Rowlands Pharmacy — all reporting losses or falls in their profits. [...] Steve Howard, quality and clinical standards director and superintendent pharmacist at LloydsPharmacy, which owns 1,597 registered pharmacies, stresses that the challenges are not only connected to funding cuts. “It is also about business rates and the apprenticeship levy, among other things,” he explains. “As the external world changes, all businesses need to adjust to the evolving landscape,” he adds.

Businesses have also been hit by a difficult retail environment and a weak pound, explains Ross Muken, senior managing director for equity research at the investment bank Evercore ISI, which analyses the stocks of Boots’s and LloydsPharmacy’s parent companies. The value of the pound sterling has fallen by 20% since the UK voted to leave the EU in June 2016.

## Challenging UK market [...] The second largest, LloydsPharmacy, has divested more than 200 pharmacies since 2016, and the fourth largest, Rowlands Pharmacy, announced in February 2019 that it plans to sell 70 of its branches.

The fact that large multiples, which make up 49.4% of the market and include companies with 100 or more pharmacies (see Infographic), are feeling the squeeze is perhaps not surprising. Like small multiples (companies with between six and 99 pharmacies) and independents, they have endured several financial challenges over the past few years.

> The current funding climate is holding back community pharmacy from its huge potential to improve outcomes for patients and reduce the pressures on GPs and [accident and emergency] departments

Budget headlines

Rachel Reeves’ first Budget was dominated by the headline figure of £40bn worth of tax rises. The changes, which are scheduled to take effect from April 6, include an increase in employer National Insurance (NI) contributions from 13.8 per cent on salaries over £9,100 to 15 per cent on salaries above £5,000.

The NI tax rise does not apply to the NHS, but this exemption has not yet been confirmed for other primary care providers, including community pharmacies, GP practices and care homes. In 2025, it is vital that pharmacies receive the right support to allow them to successfully navigate this new financial landscape. This could be achieved by strengthening government guarantee schemes to help improve SME access to finance and ensure they can manage increased costs. [...] In Scotland, changes to the Government-set tariff mechanism helped to alleviate some of the pressures. In September, Community Pharmacy Scotland (CPS) confirmed it had secured a 6 per cent funding uplift for the sector in a “long-awaited” 2024-25 funding package. CPS accepted the Scottish Government’s offer of a deal, with the guaranteed minimum for Drug Tariff reimbursement set at £110m – £10m higher than in 2023-24.

However, this positive step forward was curtailed by the delivery of Labour’s Westminster autumn Budget just one month later, which brought some expected announcements as well as a few surprises.

Budget headlines [...] Community pharmacies are key contributors to the UK economy, as well as being frontline providers of primary care. The upheaval of 2024 demonstrated that the sector is robust and responsive to change. As we enter 2025, it is vital that pharmacy owners receive the clarity and support they need to deliver their ambition – for the greater benefit of patients, communities and staff.

• Scott Hutchinson is deputy regional director (North & Scotland) and Paul Kelly is deputy regional director (South) of Unity Trust Bank.

## Shift in ownership patterns

The data also reveals a notable shift in ownership dynamics across the sector.

Small independent pharmacy owners—defined as those operating between one and five pharmacies—now hold the largest market share at over 49 per cent.

Their numbers have grown significantly from 4,024 in 2021 to 4,910 in March 2025, an increase of 886.

Medium-sized groups (owning 6 to 99 pharmacies) now account for over 18 per cent of the market, with 1,807 pharmacies recorded as of March 2025.

In contrast, large pharmacy chains (owning 100 or more pharmacies) have seen a steep decline. Their numbers have plummeted from 5,220 in 2021 to just 3,283—a reduction of 1,938.

They now represent only 32.8 per cent of the total market. [...] See Full Bio

The total number of bricks-and-mortar community pharmacies in England has dropped below 10,000, according to the latest data from the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA).

As of the end of March 2025, there were 9,999 community pharmacies (excluding distance selling pharmacies) operating in England—down from 10,837 at the beginning of 2021. This marks a net loss of 838 pharmacies over four years.

Between January 2024 and March 2025 alone, England recorded 274 pharmacy closures, averaging more than five closures per week.

When including distance selling pharmacies, the total number of pharmacies in England now stands at 10,407, down from 11,206 in January 2021.

### Pharmacy closures

Data from NHS England’s edispensary dataset suggests that over 1,000 pharmacies closed in England between February 2016 and February 2026. There were 10,526 pharmacies open in England in February 2026, compared with 11,609 in February 2016. This represents a 9% decrease (1,083 fewer pharmacies).

The reasons being cited for these closures include inadequate funding, rising operating costs and difficulty recruiting and retaining community pharmacists. [...] ### Staffing shortages

In June 2025, Community Pharmacy England published its Pharmacy Pressures Survey: Medicines Supply Report after surveying 4,300 owners and head office representatives, and 1,600 pharmacy team members.

60% of pharmacy teams reported staffing shortages. 54% of pharmacy owners reported struggling to recruit permanent staff. 81% of pharmacy staff reported longer patient waiting times, and 57% said they had a reduced ability to offer advice and services.

# Almost five million Pharmacy First consultations delivered in first year

A man and an older lady stand at a pharmacy counter 

SolStock / E+ via Getty Images

Almost five million Pharmacy First consultations were delivered in the first year of the service in England, official data has confirmed.

The latest data from the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA) shows that contractors in England submitted claims for 4,941,308 Pharmacy First consultations between February 2024 and January 2025.

Of those, more than half (2,735,577) were referred into pharmacies from GP surgeries or NHS111 and were claimed as minor illness or urgent medicine supply referrals. [...] In January 2025, contractors had to complete 25 clinical pathway consultations to be eligible for the £1,000 monthly payment – an increase from the 20 required in December.

The increase meant that fewer contractors were able to meet the threshold, and just 4,940 contractors were eligible for the monthly payment in January – down from 6,194 the month before.

Overall, 9,265, or 87% of contractors in England, delivered at least one Pharmacy First consultation in January 2025, suggesting that the service is active in almost nine in ten pharmacies.

Tase Oputu, chair of the England board of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society (RPS), said the figures ‘show the real impact Pharmacy First is having, with millions of patients getting faster access to care and easing pressure on GPs.’ [...] He said the service was ‘an important stepping stone towards a more clinical future’, and CPE was advocating for the service to include more clinical pathways and independent prescribing in the future.

Total numbers of both clinical pathway and referral consultations dropped slightly in January 2025 after reaching their highest levels yet in December 2024.

Nick Thayer, head of policy, told The Pharmacist that it was ‘common to see spikes of Pharmacy First consultations around bank holidays and when other providers may not be readily accessible’.

And he cited analysis of CCA pharmacies that found a 15% increase in activity during the CrowdStrike IT outage in July 2024 and a 10% increase in activity in the week leading up to Christmas.

# NHS England Pharmacy First Payment Caps — Second-Order Effects Dossier (March 2026 Onward)

## Background & Context

The NHS Pharmacy First Service (PFS), launched 31 January 2024, was designed to divert an estimated 10 million minor-illness consultations annually away from GP surgeries into community pharmacies, covering seven (soon expanding) clinical pathways: acute otitis media, acute sore throat, impetigo, infected insect bites, shingles, sinusitis, and uncomplicated UTIs in women [22]. Uptake has exceeded expectations: consultations rose from 125,275/month in February 2024 to 254,692/month by June 2025 [21], with over 3.3 million consultations delivered between March 2025 and February 2026 — a 43% year-on-year increase [3][7]. Over 10,900 pharmacies (of roughly 10,526–10,900 remaining in England) now participate [17].

The core tension: NHS England's payment model pays a fixed monthly sum (£500 for 20-29 consultations; £1,000 for 30+) [4][5][10] rather than uncapped fee-for-service. As volumes have grown faster than the funding envelope, NHS England has introduced **hard monthly caps** on the number of consultations for which any contractor can be paid, banded by each pharmacy's own historic delivery volume [1]. Crucially, the caps are **tightening over time**: a Band 6 (highest-volume, 47+ consultations/month) pharmacy could claim payment for up to 234 consultations/month in the March 2026 schedule, but this falls to 149 by the February 2026 schedule and just 120 by April 2026 [1] — a rapid, multi-step ratchet down within a matter of weeks, reflecting NHS England's attempt to control a runaway demand-side budget line within a fixed overall CPCF envelope of £3.636 billion for 2026/27 (up 10.3%/£340m from £3.296bn) [5][6][9][10].

This is happening against a backdrop of:
- A record-low pharmacy count: 9,999 bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16], rising slightly to 10,526 by February 2026 but still 9% below February 2016 levels [17].
- Severe staffing pressure: 60% of pharmacy teams report staffing shortages, 54% of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff, 81% of staff report longer patient waits, 57% report reduced ability to give advice [17].
- A structural shift in ownership from large multiples (down from 5,220 pharmacies in 2021 to 3,283, i.e. 32.8% market share) toward small independents (up from 4,024 to 4,910, now 49%+ market share) [16].
- Continued "financial crisis" framing by the sector's negotiating body, Community Pharmacy England (CPE), even after securing the 10.3% uplift, which it says will cover "growth in activity and inflation... but will not make further progress towards delivering sustainability" [5][10][14].

The central policy tension for simulation purposes: **NHS England needs to cap an open-ended, successful, patient-popular service to protect a fixed budget, while pharmacy contractors — especially high-volume, high fixed-cost operators — see their marginal consultations effectively become unpaid labour, creating a perverse incentive to slow-walk or turn away exactly the patients the policy was designed to attract.**

## Key Stakeholders

**NHS England (Commissioner)**
- Stated position: Pharmacy First is a flagship success reducing GP/A&E pressure; caps are a "fair" mechanism to manage a fixed budget as volumes scale; funding rose 10.3% for 2026/27 [5][9].
- Underlying interest: Controlling in-year budget exposure; avoiding a repeat of prior "over-delivery" episodes requiring later clawback/write-off (as happened with the £239m medicines margin write-off) [10]; managing optics of a wildly popular scheme becoming fiscally unsustainable.
- Influence: High (sole commissioner, sets banding methodology, controls Drug Tariff).
- Communication style: Technocratic, table-and-band driven official notices via NHSBSA bulletins; avoids overt acknowledgment of access-restricting effects; frames changes as "banded approach" management rather than rationing.
- Rhetorical pattern: Emphasises aggregate consultation totals and funding uplift percentages; downplays per-contractor marginal economics.

**Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) / Secretary of State for Health and Social Care (Wes Streeting, as of the period covered)**
- Stated position: Champion of "neighbourhood health service" model in the NHS 10-Year Health Plan; wants community pharmacy to absorb more primary care demand, including the autumn 2026 independent prescribing (IP) expansion funded by £340m [3][7][5].
- Underlying interest: Political credit for cutting GP waiting times and A&E pressure without raising taxes; needs pharmacy sector cooperative rather than openly hostile ahead of elections; wants to show fiscal discipline amid £225bn NHS Spending Review envelope [5].
- Influence: High (sets overall NHS funding envelope, political accountability).
- Communication style: Upbeat, expansion-focused press releases; contract announcements framed as "one of the largest budget uplifts across the NHS."
- Rhetorical pattern: Cites cumulative consultation totals (3.3m, 5m, 5.4m milestones) [3][22] as proof of success while structural underfunding critique from CPE is acknowledged only obliquely.

**Community Pharmacy England (CPE)** — the statutory negotiating body for contractors
- Stated position: Accepted the 2026/27 deal as "best chance of a better future" but explicitly warns of an "ongoing crisis in pharmacies" [10]; wants deeper structural reform, not just funding uplifts.
- Underlying interest: Represents ~10,500 contractors with sharply divergent interests (large multiples vs. independents); must balance confrontation against the risk of losing members' confidence if it appears too compliant with NHS England.
- Influence: High (sole negotiating body, publishes the influential Pressures Survey [14][17]).
- Communication style: Careful, dual-track messaging — welcomes funding headline figures while publishing survey data emphasizing crisis (financial losses, patient care delays) [14].
- Rhetorical pattern: "Warns Government about the ongoing crisis... but decides constructive joint work on reform is essential" [10] — classic insider/outsider hybrid stance.

**Large Pharmacy Multiples: Boots, LloydsPharmacy (owned by Bestway since 2022), Well Pharmacy, Rowlands Pharmacy (Phoenix Group)**
- Stated position: Publicly supportive of Pharmacy First's clinical ambition; privately warn of business rates, apprenticeship levy, NI increases, and margin pressure "not only connected to funding cuts" [12].
- Underlying interest: These operators run highest-volume branches (more likely Band 5/6, thus first and hardest hit by the falling caps); need consultation volume to justify pharmacist headcount, but caps make marginal consultations unpaid — creates strong incentive to redistribute or ration PF slots across a chain, or deprioritise walk-ins once the monthly cap is reached.
- Influence: High economically (49.4% market share historically, though declining), but reputationally exposed as "profiteering" targets in media narratives.
- Communication style: Corporate, cautious, spokesperson-mediated (e.g., Steve Howard, LloydsPharmacy's superintendent pharmacist, quoted on rates/levy issues) [12].
- Rhetorical pattern: Frames issues as "external world changing" and "adjusting to evolving landscape" rather than direct criticism of NHS England — reputational risk aversion.
- Note: Large chains have been net sellers of branches (LloydsPharmacy divested 200+ since 2016; Rowlands announced sale of 70 in Feb 2019) [12], a trend continuing into 2025 with "corporate and multiple operators account[ing] for 71.3 percent of all sales instructions year to date" [13] — i.e., consolidation reversal, chains shrinking, independents/first-time buyers absorbing stock.

**Independent Pharmacy Owners / Small Multiples (1-5 branches, now 49%+ of market)**
- Stated position: Represented informally by figures like Fin McCaul (Greater Manchester-based independent contractor, quoted by CPE) [14], who emphasize community and workforce impact of closures.
- Underlying interest: Lower fixed-cost base than multiples but thinner cash reserves; a single pharmacy hitting its cap has nowhere to redistribute unpaid consultations; disproportionately exposed to "one bad month" volume risk (banding based on trailing 3-month averages means a temporary demand spike, e.g. flu season, doesn't get proportionally rewarded).
- Influence: Medium individually, but numerically dominant and politically sympathetic ("save the local pharmacy" narrative resonates with local MPs and high-street regeneration agendas).
- Communication style: Personal, anecdotal, often via CPE press statements or local media ("what closure of the business would mean for their staff... local high streets, some of which could not survive another vacant building" [14]).
- Rhetorical pattern: Community/high-street framing; existential ("crisis," "unsustainable," "pathway to a sustainable future" [14]).

**General Practitioners (GPs) / Royal College of GPs (RCGP) / BMA GP Committee**
- Stated position: Cautiously supportive of Pharmacy First diverting minor-illness demand but concerned about clinical safety, referral loops, and the informal expectation that GPs "backstop" pharmacy caps once a pharmacy has hit its monthly quota (patients bounced back to GP practices when pharmacies stop accepting PF referrals).
- Underlying interest: GPs are themselves under contract-funding strain; do not want to reabsorb the ~10 million appointments PF was meant to free up [21]; want credit for referrals into PF (GP-referred PF consultations count toward practice QOF-adjacent workload metrics).
- Influence: Medium-high (physician voice carries clinical authority, RCGP/BMA statements attract media pick-up).
- Communication style: Cautious, evidence-request framing (want data on referral patterns, safety-netting); prior reporting shows "significant variation in GP referrals to Pharmacy First across England" [22] — a known unknown ripe for controversy.
- Rhetorical pattern: "Urgent reform needed to fulfil Pharmacy First potential" [22] — measured, reform-oriented rather than oppositional.

**NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA)**
- Stated position: Administrative/data body; publishes bands, caps, contractor lists monthly [1][2].
- Underlying interest: Operational execution, not policy; wants clean, low-dispute payment reconciliation.
- Influence: Medium (implements policy, but doesn't set it); high information-asymmetry power since it alone determines individual contractor bands.
- Communication style: Purely technical/tabular bulletins; the most granular and "ground truth" source for band assignment disputes.

**Patients (Segmented)**
- Working-age patients with minor ailments: benefit from fast access, avoid GP wait times; increasingly rely on Pharmacy First as the "front door" to NHS primary care.
- Prescription-charge-liable patients: pay £9.90 per item (2026 standard charge) [3] even though the consultation itself is free — a friction point especially once independent prescribing broadens the range of conditions treated.
- Exempt patients (children, over-60s, pregnant women, low-income): the caps' access effects fall hardest on non-exempt working-age adults if pharmacies start rationing slots.
- Patients in deprived / pharmacy-desert areas: most exposed to closures given closures concentrated in areas with weaker commercial viability (implied by closure data trends [16][17], consistent with pre-existing "pharmacy deserts" literature).
- Influence: Low individually, but aggregated patient satisfaction/access data (waiting times, "closed to Pharmacy First" signage) is highly salient in local press and social media — the most powerful "swing" narrative constituency.

- Stated position: Operational conduits relaying NHSBSA guidance to contractors ("Community Pharmacy Tracker" reminders about claim deadlines and cap checks [2]).
- Underlying interest: Want contractors compliant and paid correctly; avoid missed claim windows (a recurring failure mode given the historically short one-month claim window, now extended to three months from June 2026 [5][9]).
- Influence: Medium (trusted intermediary, but no negotiating power of their own).

- Stated position (inferred from historical pattern and [12]): Lobbies for funding sufficient to cover multiples' higher cost base (business rates, apprenticeship levy, NI).
- Underlying interest: Protect scale economics; may quietly favour caps if they curb "gaming" by aggressive independent operators overclaiming, but oppose caps that penalise their own high-volume flagship branches.
- Influence: High (represents ~32.8% market share but disproportionate media/lobbying access).

## Reaction Chains & Decision Dynamics

**If NHS England proceeds with the scheduled cap reductions (Band 6 max falling from 234 → 149 → 120 consultations/month across March–April 2026):**
- High-volume independents and multiple branches likely respond by **soft-rationing**: reception staff start declining or deferring walk-in Pharmacy First requests once the pharmacy nears its monthly cap, redirecting patients back to GP practices or 111.
- CPE is likely to escalate publicly via its Pressures Survey mechanism [14], using patient-impact framing ("delays to medicines and reduced access to care") to pressure DHSC ahead of the next contractual round.
- Large multiples (Boots, Well, Lloyds, Rowlands) likely respond by **reallocating pharmacist hours away from PF-heavy branches** toward branches with headroom under their band, or by centralising PF delivery in fewer "hub" branches — accelerating closures/consolidation in marginal branches per the ownership-shift trend already visible in the data [16].
- GPs likely see a partial rebound in minor-illness appointment requests once pharmacies hit caps mid-month, undermining the "10 million appointments freed" narrative and giving RCGP/BMA ammunition to argue PF has hit a structural ceiling.

**If a high-profile patient-harm or "turned away" story goes viral (e.g., a sepsis-linked UTI or a child not treated due to a pharmacy being "closed to Pharmacy First" mid-month):**
- DHSC/Secretary of State likely responds defensively, citing aggregate uplift figures (£340m, 43% growth) and may commission an urgent NHSBSA review of band methodology.
- Opposition MPs and Select Committee members likely call for an emergency evidence session; NAO/PAC scrutiny of the banding formula becomes likely within 2-3 months.
- CPE likely uses the moment to push for uncapped fee-for-service restoration, citing patient safety rather than contractor economics (more persuasive framing).

**If independent prescribing (IP) expansion proceeds from autumn 2026 as planned [3][5][7]:**
- Pharmacies not participating in IP face a *separate, likely lower* cap band under the dual-cap structure confirmed in the 2026/27 contract [5], creating a two-tier market: IP-enabled pharmacies (extra £525/month infrastructure fee + £500 one-off) able to sustain higher volumes profitably, non-IP pharmacies increasingly marginalised.
- Expect independents with limited capital to under-invest in IP set-up costs relative to multiples, worsening the independent/multiple divergence and potentially reversing the current independent market-share gains.
- Workforce attrition risk rises: pharmacists asked to take on prescribing scope without commensurate pay uplift may seek higher-paying locum or hospital-sector roles, intensifying the already-reported 54% recruitment struggle [17].

**If NHS England is seen to be "clawing back" or under-crediting contractors near their cap (perception of a hard cliff-edge rather than gradual taper):**
- Independent owners are the most likely to escalate to media/local MP complaints (lower institutional capacity to absorb a bad month vs. multiples' central finance teams).
- CPE likely formalises a request for a smoothing mechanism (e.g., quarterly rather than monthly banding) at the next contractual negotiation cycle.

**If patient demand continues to grow at ~40%+ YoY [3][7] while caps tighten:**
- A structural mismatch emerges: total patient demand for PF outstrips the total *paid* capacity implied by aggregate caps across all bands — creating de facto **unpaid consultation delivery** by contractors who continue seeing patients out of professional obligation/goodwill, an unsustainable "free labour" dynamic that CPE will use as its central grievance narrative in future negotiations.

## Public Opinion Landscape

- **Pro-Pharmacy First patient-access narrative**: "Fast, free, local care" — resonant with parents, working adults; hashtag-style framing likely to emerge as "#PharmacyFirst" success stories vs "#PharmacyCrisis" closures. Polling proxy: 3.3m consultations/year and 43% YoY growth [3][7] indicate strong genuine demand — this is the dominant, still-strengthening narrative among patients and the DHSC/NHS England communications machine.
- **Pharmacy financial crisis narrative**: Driven by CPE's Pressures Survey [14][17] — "patients increasingly feeling the impact through delays to medicines and reduced access to care." This is a rising narrative, gaining traction particularly in trade press (Pharmaceutical Journal, Pharmacy Business, The Pharmacist) and likely to break into mainstream press if closures accelerate past the current ~5/week rate [16].
- **"Bureaucratic rationing" narrative**: Framing the banding/cap system as a stealth rationing mechanism — likely to be pushed by CPE and independent contractors once contractors realise their marginal consultations go unpaid; could develop into a "hidden NHS waiting list" story analogous to past GP-access controversies.
- **Fiscal responsibility narrative**: NHS England/DHSC framing that caps are a "necessary and fair" mechanism to manage an unprecedented surge in a demand-led budget within a constrained overall settlement (£225bn NHS Spending Review) [5] — likely to hold steady among Treasury-aligned commentators but is a minority, technocratic narrative with limited social-media traction.
- **Workforce burnout narrative**: From pharmacist unions/PDA-type voices — "unsustainable workload without matching pay," echoing broader NHS staffing narratives (junior doctors, nurses) — polarising, since it invites comparison to other NHS workforce disputes and potential solidarity/strike-adjacent framing (though pharmacy contractors are self-employed/small business owners, not directly unionised in the same way).
- **Consolidation/"pharmacy deserts" narrative**: Local news framing around specific closures — "last pharmacy in town closes" stories — high emotional resonance, likely amplified by local MPs regardless of party, cutting across the polarised national funding debate.

Overall polarisation is **rising but not yet acute**: this is a technical, sector-specific dispute rather than a hot-button partisan issue, but it has clear escalation pathways (patient harm story, mass closure wave, high-profile multiple exiting the PF scheme entirely) that could push it into mainstream political discourse within the March–autumn 2026 window.

## Information Flow & Influence Networks

- **Primary source layer**: NHSBSA official bulletins and Excel cap lists [1] → picked up by trade press (Pharmaceutical Journal [9], The Pharmacist [5][21], Pharmacy Business [13][16]) within days.
- **CPE as amplifier and translator**: CPE's press releases [10][14] reframe raw NHSBSA/DHSC data into sector-narrative terms ("crisis," "sustainability") — these statements are the primary quotable source for both trade press and any mainstream pickup.
- **Local Pharmaceutical Committees** relay operational detail (claim windows, band checks) directly to contractors via trackers like the CPSC Community Pharmacy Tracker [2] — this is the "last mile" compliance channel, largely invisible to public discourse but critical to whether contractors actually optimise/game their banding.
- **Trade press → mainstream press cascade**: Pharmacy Business and Pharmaceutical Journal stories on closures [16][17] are the most likely vector for mainstream pickup (BBC, Guardian, Daily Mail health sections historically amplify "closure of the local pharmacy" stories), especially when tied to constituency-level MP comment.
- **Corporate multiples' communication**: Filtered through spokespeople (e.g., Steve Howard at LloydsPharmacy [12]) and investor calls covered by financial analysts (Evercore ISI's Ross Muken [12]) — this channel primarily reaches financial/trade audiences, rarely mainstream, unless tied to a large-scale closure announcement (e.g., "Boots to close X stores").
- **Patient-level amplification**: Social media (Twitter/X, Facebook local community groups, Mumsnet-style parenting forums) is the likely vector for individual "I was turned away" anecdotes — these are high-virality, low-verification stories that can rapidly reframe the aggregate-success narrative pushed by DHSC.
- **Political amplification**: Health and Social Care Select Committee, shadow health ministers, and RCGP/BMA statements provide the escalation path from sector press to Parliamentary scrutiny — House of Commons Library briefings [17] indicate Parliament is already actively tracking closures and staffing data as of March 2026, suggesting this is primed for a Select Committee hearing trigger.

## Quantitative Anchors

- CPCF total funding 2026/27: **£3.636 billion**, up from £3.296bn in 2025/26 — **10.3% (£340m) uplift** [5][6][9][10].
- Pharmacy First budget now folded into CPCF (previously separate £215m line in 2025/26; £8m digital developments also folded in) [6].
- Prior year (2025/26) uplift was **19.7%** — so 2026/27's 10.3% represents a marked deceleration [5][9].
- Margin allowance uplift: **£200 million** added to annual margin, taking retained margin to **£1.1 billion** [10].
- Historic over-delivery write-off: **up to £239 million** (up to end of March 2026) [6][10], following a prior **£193 million** write-off agreed for 2024/25 [8].
- Single Activity Fee (SAF): rose from £1.27 → £1.46 (April 2025) [8] → **£1.52** (backdated to May 2026) [9].
- Pharmacy First consultation fee: rose from £15 → **£17** [4].
- Banded fixed payments: **£500** for 20-29 consultations/month; **£1,000** for 30+ consultations/month [2][4][5].
- Prescription charge (2026): **£9.90 per item** [3].
- Independent prescribing (IP) set-up: **£500 one-off fee** + **£525/month infrastructure fee** per contractor [5].
- IP expansion funding: **£340 million** government deal for autumn 2026 rollout [3][7].
- Consultation volumes: **3.3 million** PF consultations March 2025–Feb 2026 (**+43% YoY**) [3][7]; **2.75 million** clinical pathway consultations April 2025–Jan 2026 [6]; **~1 million** contraception consultations and **~3 million** hypertension case-finding consultations in the same 10-month window [6]; **~1 billion** prescription items dispensed in the same period [6]; **254,692** PF consultations/month by June 2025, up from **125,275**/month in Feb 2024 [21]; **5.4 million** cumulative PF consultations Jan 2024–Feb 2025 [22]; **4.5 million** consultations claimed Feb 2024–Oct 2025 [17].
- Pharmacy count: **9,999** bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16]; **10,526** as of February 2026 (down 9% / 1,083 fewer than Feb 2016's 11,609) [17]; **10,900** participating in PF as of October 2025 [17].
- Closures: **274 closures** Jan 2024–March 2025 (>5/week average) [16]; **~1,000+ closures** Feb 2016–Feb 2026 [17].
- Ownership shift: small independents (1-5 branches) grew from **4,024 (2021) → 4,910 (March 2025)**, now **49%+ market share**; large chains (100+) fell from **5,220 (2021) → 3,283**, now **32.8% market share**; medium groups (6-99) at **18%+ / 1,807 pharmacies** [16].
- Staffing: **60%** of pharmacy teams report shortages; **54%** of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff; **81%** report longer patient waits; **57%** report reduced ability to give advice (CPE Pharmacy Pressures Survey, June 2025, n=4,300 owners/head-office reps + 1,600 team members) [17].
- Band caps (March 2026 schedule): Band 1 (<18/month avg) capped at 45 paid; Band 6 (47+/month avg) capped at 234 paid [1]. By April 2026 schedule, Band 6 cap falls to just **120** [1] — a **~49% reduction** in the space of two monthly schedule updates.
- Employer NI rise (Budget effective April 2025): **13.8% → 15%** on salaries above a lowered £5,000 threshold (from £9,100) [15] — NHS-exempt but pharmacy contractor status uncertain/likely non-exempt, a major cost pressure compounding cap effects.
- Tax rise flagged for pharmacy business sales: **4% tax increase** from April 2026 affecting exit/succession planning [11].

## Historical Precedents

1. **Medicines margin over-delivery and clawback cycles (2019-2024)**: Historic precedent for the same dynamic now seen with PF caps — the sector over-delivered against fixed margin assumptions, prompting negotiated write-offs (£193m in 2024/25 [8], up to £239m by 2026 [6][10]) rather than punitive recovery. This suggests DHSC/NHS England's playbook when a demand-led scheme outruns its budget is to eventually forgive over-delivery rather than claw back — a precedent contractors will cite when lobbying against the PF caps, arguing caps are unnecessary if clawback can simply be written off later. Timeline: ~5 years of recurring settlement cycles. Outcome: sector avoided existential clawback each time, but funding uncertainty entrenched.

2. **Community Pharmacist Consultation Service (CPCS) to Pharmacy First transition (2019-2024)**: PF absorbed and rebranded the CPCS, itself introduced to redirect NHS 111/GP referrals to pharmacy. This is a close structural precedent — a previous minor-illness referral scheme that also faced volume/funding tension before being restructured into PF with clinical pathways and formulary. Degree of mirror: high — same actors (NHS England, CPE, GPs), same fundamental tension (fixed budget vs. variable demand), resolved via rebrand/expansion rather than genuine funding fix.

3. **GP contract "QOF" (Quality and Outcomes Framework) capping and gaming dynamics**: GPs have long experience of activity-based payment schemes with thresholds/caps producing "threshold gaming" (patients coded just below/above payment cut-offs). Close analogy for how PF banding could produce pharmacy-level gaming: contractors may adjust reported consultation timing/eligibility near month-end to optimise which band they fall into for the *next* period, given caps are set from trailing 3-month averages [1]. Degree of mirror: medium-high — same perverse-incentive structure, different sector.

4. **Large multiple divestment wave (2016-2019)**: LloydsPharmacy divested 200+ branches since 2016; Rowlands announced 70-branch sale in Feb 2019 [12], driven by post-Brexit sterling weakness (-20% vs. pre-2016 [12]), business rates, and funding pressure. Directly analogous precedent for the current cap-driven pressure on multiples: history shows multiples respond to margin squeeze not by campaigning loudly but by quietly shedding branches — expect the same "silent exit" pattern (branch sales to independents/first-time buyers) rather than public confrontation, consistent with 2025 data showing corporates behind 71.3% of sale instructions [13].

5. **Community Pharmacy Scotland 2024-25 settlement (6% uplift, £110m guaranteed minimum)** [15]: A comparator jurisdiction showing a smaller, more modest but "long-awaited" negotiated settlement model — useful for benchmarking whether England's CPE-DHSC dynamic could shift toward the Scottish model of guaranteed minimum funding without volume caps, which CPE could invoke as an alternative model in future negotiations.

6. **NHS dentistry access crisis (2021-2024)**: The most politically potent precedent — capped NHS dental contract "Units of Dental Activity" led to widespread practice withdrawal from NHS work, "dental deserts," and became a significant national media and electoral issue (dental access was a top-5 local election issue in 2023-24). Degree of mirror: high cautionary tale — if PF caps produce a similar "contractors quietly stop offering the NHS service once their cap is hit" dynamic, pharmacy could follow dentistry's trajectory into a nationally salient access crisis within 1-2 years. This is the most important wildcard precedent for the simulation to weight heavily.

## Key Risk Factors & Wildcards

- **Cliff-edge rationing**: Contractors stop accepting PF walk-ins once their monthly cap is reached, creating visible mid-month "closed to Pharmacy First" signage — a highly shareable, negative social-media trigger.
- **Patient harm incident**: A serious clinical outcome (e.g., missed sepsis, delayed antibiotic for a child) linked to a patient being turned away or delayed due to cap-related rationing — would likely trigger a Select Committee inquiry and emergency DHSC statement within days.
- **Mass independent closures**: If closures accelerate beyond the ~5/week baseline [16], local MP pressure (cross-party) could force an early review of banding methodology before the scheduled 2027/28 Pharmacy Access Scheme review [9].
- **Multiple exits PF scheme entirely**: A large chain (e.g., Boots or Well) publicly withdrawing from PF in select loss-making regions would be a major escalation, converting a slow-burn financial story into an acute national access story.
- **Gaming/fraud allegations**: Banding based on trailing consultation averages creates incentive to inflate Oct-Dec reporting period volumes to secure a higher future cap — NHS Counter Fraud Authority scrutiny is a plausible wildcard, especially given historic margin over-delivery write-off patterns [6][8][10].
- **Workforce attrition acceleration**: With 54% of owners already struggling to recruit [17], compounding pressure from IP scope expansion without matching pay could accelerate pharmacist emigration to Australia/Canada (a known historical pattern) or moves into more lucrative locum/hospital roles.
- **Political timing risk**: Any Spending Review or Budget re-opening (especially given the "4% tax increase... April 2026" [11] and broader NI changes) could force DHSC to revisit the CPCF settlement mid-year, destabilising contractor planning.

data.simulation_requirement: Model the second-order effects of NHS England payment caps on Pharmacy First consultations from March 2026: pharmacy multiples, independents, GPs, patients, NHS England — financial strain, patient access, workforce attrition, policy escalation.

data.prompt: Model the second-order effects of NHS England payment caps on Pharmacy First consultations from March 2026: pharmacy multiples, independents, GPs, patients, NHS England — financial strain, patient access, workforce attrition, policy escalation.

key_facts: A record-low pharmacy count: 9,999 bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16], rising slightly to 10,526 by February 2026 but still 9% below February 2016 levels [17].

Severe staffing pressure: 60% of pharmacy teams report staffing shortages, 54% of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff, 81% of staff report longer patient waits, 57% report reduced ability to give advice [17].

A structural shift in ownership from large multiples (down from 5,220 pharmacies in 2021 to 3,283, i.e. 32.8% market share) toward small independents (up from 4,024 to 4,910, now 49%+ market share) [16].

Continued "financial crisis" framing by the sector's negotiating body, Community Pharmacy England (CPE), even after securing the 10.3% uplift, which it says will cover "growth in activity and inflation... but will not make further progress towards delivering sustainability" [5][10][14].
quantitative_anchors: Pharmacy First budget now folded into CPCF (previously separate £215m line in 2025/26; £8m digital developments also folded in) [6].
Prior year (2025/26) uplift was **19.7%** — so 2026/27's 10.3% represents a marked deceleration [5][9].
Margin allowance uplift: **£200 million** added to annual margin, taking retained margin to **£1.1 billion** [10].
Historic over-delivery write-off: **up to £239 million** (up to end of March 2026) [6][10], following a prior **£193 million** write-off agreed for 2024/25 [8].
Single Activity Fee (SAF): rose from £1.27 → £1.46 (April 2025) [8] → **£1.52** (backdated to May 2026) [9].
Pharmacy First consultation fee: rose from £15 → **£17** [4].
Banded fixed payments: **£500** for 20-29 consultations/month; **£1,000** for 30+ consultations/month [2][4][5].
Prescription charge (2026): **£9.90 per item** [3].
Independent prescribing (IP) set-up: **£500 one-off fee** + **£525/month infrastructure fee** per contractor [5].
IP expansion funding: **£340 million** government deal for autumn 2026 rollout [3][7].

Consultation volumes: **3.3 million** PF consultations March 2025–Feb 2026 (**+43% YoY**) [3][7]; **2.75 million** clinical pathway consultations April 2025–Jan 2026 [6]; **~1 million** contraception consultations and **~3 million** hypertension case-finding consultations in the same 10-month window [6]; **~1 billion** prescription items dispensed in the same period [6]; **254,692** PF consultations/month by June 2025, up from **125,275**/month in Feb 2024 [21]; **5.4 million** cumulative PF consultations Jan 2024–Feb 2025 [22]; **4.5 million** consultations claimed Feb 2024–Oct 2025 [17].

Pharmacy count: **9,999** bricks-and-mortar pharmacies in England as of March 2025 (down from 10,837 in Jan 2021) [16]; **10,526** as of February 2026 (down 9% / 1,083 fewer than Feb 2016's 11,609) [17]; **10,900** participating in PF as of October 2025 [17].
Closures: **274 closures** Jan 2024–March 2025 (>5/week average) [16]; **~1,000+ closures** Feb 2016–Feb 2026 [17].

Ownership shift: small independents (1-5 branches) grew from **4,024 (2021) → 4,910 (March 2025)**, now **49%+ market share**; large chains (100+) fell from **5,220 (2021) → 3,283**, now **32.8% market share**; medium groups (6-99) at **18%+ / 1,807 pharmacies** [16].

Staffing: **60%** of pharmacy teams report shortages; **54%** of owners struggle to recruit permanent staff; **81%** report longer patient waits; **57%** report reduced ability to give advice (CPE Pharmacy Pressures Survey, June 2025, n=4,300 owners/head-office reps + 1,600 team members) [17].

Band caps (March 2026 schedule): Band 1 (<18/month avg) capped at 45 paid; Band 6 (47+/month avg) capped at 234 paid [1]. By April 2026 schedule, Band 6 cap falls to just **120** [1] — a **~49% reduction** in the space of two monthly schedule updates.

Employer NI rise (Budget effective April 2025): **13.8% → 15%** on salaries above a lowered £5,000 threshold (from £9,100) [15] — NHS-exempt but pharmacy contractor status uncertain/likely non-exempt, a major cost pressure compounding cap effects.
Tax rise flagged for pharmacy business sales: **4% tax increase** from April 2026 affecting exit/succession planning [11].

## What are the costs and who is exempt?

The pharmacist consultation itself is free on the NHS. However, any medicine supplied under Pharmacy First is subject to normal NHS prescription charges. As of 2026, the standard prescription charge is £9.90 per item. This is the same charge you would pay for a medicine collected from a GP prescription.

The table below summarises who pays and who is exempt: [...] | Major expansion from autumn 2026 | A £340 million government deal enables independent pharmacist prescribing, building on 3.3 million consultations delivered in one year. | [...] The scale of existing demand makes this expansion logical. Between March 2025 and February 2026, over 3.3 million consultations were delivered under Pharmacy First in England, representing a 43% increase year on year. That figure reflects genuine patient appetite for accessible, fast, pharmacist-led care. The expansion is designed to meet that demand while simultaneously reducing pressure on GP surgeries and A&E departments.

sources.title: CPCF Overview 2026-27

sources.content:
The current capping mechanism for Pharmacy First consultations will be retained, and a similar approach will be used for IP consultations. This means there will be two caps within each band: one applicable to pharmacies signed up to provide prescribing services, and one for those who are not offering the new prescribing services.

Fixed payments will remain at £500 for contractors delivering 20 to 29 consultations in a month and £1,000 for those delivering 30 consultations or more, regardless of whether they are prescribing consultations or not.

CPE also agreed a two-month late claim window for Pharmacy First and the New Medicine Service (NMS) – the two advanced services that still have a one-month claim window – giving contractors a total of three months to make a claim. [...] The DHSC said the initial introduction of independent prescribing during 2026/27 will be funded through a one-off £500 set-up fee, payable once a contractor has signed up to deliver the relevant service, and a £525 monthly infrastructure fee.

CPE said that bacterial conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis, oral thrush, skin infections and respiratory tract infections are services that would be considered for the expanded Pharmacy First service.

During the summer, NHS England will create a clinical reference group of experts across primary care who will consider the new pathways for IPs under Pharmacy First, The Pharmacist understands. [...] ## A £340 million funding uplift

The headline funding announcement is that community pharmacy funding will rise by £340 million funding in 2026/27 after Community Pharmacy England (CPE) accepted the government’s offer.

This will see the sector’s budget increase by 10.3% to £3.636 billion – higher than the NHS overall increase of 2.7%, but significantly lower than last year’s 19.7% funding boost.

The Pharmacist understands that this is not new money but will come from the total NHS funding (£225bn) announced at the 2026/27 Spending Review.

CPE has warned that the new funding will cover growth in activity and inflation in the coming year but will not make further progress towards delivering sustainability to the sector.
sources.title: What does the 2026/27 contract mean for pharmacies? - The Pharmacist

sources.content:
## CPCF funding changes

As outlined above, CPCF and Pharmacy First funding will increase from £3.296 billion in 2025 to 2026 to £3.636 billion in the financial year of 2026 to 2027. We will also write off up to £239 million of historic net contract over-delivery against the historic settlements.

Table 1: changes to available funding, 2025 to 2026 to 2026 to 2027

| 2025 to 2026 | 2026 to 2027 |
 --- |
| CPCF (£ billion) | 3.073 | 3.636 |
| Pharmacy First (£ million) | 215 | Included in CPCF |
| Digital developments (£ million) | 8 | Included in CPCF |

# Q1 2025 Pharmacy Market Update

## Momentum Builds Despite Sector Headwinds.

The UK pharmacy market entered 2025 with a surprising surge in acquisition activity. Despite broader economic pressures – including stubborn inflation, ongoing NHS funding constraints and increasing costs as a result of the previous Labour budget – buyer demand for community pharmacies has sharply increased.

Q1 saw a noticeable uptick in average offers based on EBITDA multiples, faster transaction timelines, and renewed confidence from both multiples and independent operators.

### Buyer Activity on the Rise [...] Working in partnership with Prospect Health, one of the UKs largest healthcare recruitment specialists, Prospect Estates have unrivalled access to pharmacists looking to move in to ownership and we’re well placed to keep you in tune with first-time buyer trends and patterns.

Q1 2025 Pharmacy Market Update

### Sector Challenges and the New Pharmacy Contract

This uptick comes amid real challenges. The UK pharmacy sector continues to navigate staffing challenges, rising costs, and increased clinical service expectations under the new 2025/26 Community Pharmacy Contractual Framework (CPCF). While the contract brings welcome clarity and modest funding increases for clinical services, many pharmacy owners are still under pressure to do more with less. [...] However, this very environment is also prompting a wave of consolidation. Some owners are choosing to exit while valuations are holding, while buyers are banking on long-term upside as the role of community pharmacy in primary care expands.

### Our verdict

The outlook for the pharmacy market for the remainder of 2025 looks positive so far – you can follow our blog posts for regular updates and perceived changes.

We urge anyone considering their short and mid-term exit strategy to be mindful of the 4% tax increases coming in April 2026. Whilst the speed of pharmacy transaction has increased, it’s advisable for owners to plan their timelines, and get their ducks in a row, well in advance of a sale becoming a reality.

# Large multiples: feeling the financial squeeze

How the UK’s four largest community pharmacy chains are coping with the current financial climate and the strategies they are employing to tackle the challenges it brings.

Large pharmacy crosses

Julie Lee / The Pharmaceutical Journal

Great Britain’s big pharmacy chains may be able to leverage economies of scale but they are not immune to the financial climate affecting the sector, with the four largest — Boots, LloydsPharmacy, Well Pharmacy and Rowlands Pharmacy — all reporting losses or falls in their profits. [...] Steve Howard, quality and clinical standards director and superintendent pharmacist at LloydsPharmacy, which owns 1,597 registered pharmacies, stresses that the challenges are not only connected to funding cuts. “It is also about business rates and the apprenticeship levy, among other things,” he explains. “As the external world changes, all businesses need to adjust to the evolving landscape,” he adds.

Businesses have also been hit by a difficult retail environment and a weak pound, explains Ross Muken, senior managing director for equity research at the investment bank Evercore ISI, which analyses the stocks of Boots’s and LloydsPharmacy’s parent companies. The value of the pound sterling has fallen by 20% since the UK voted to leave the EU in June 2016.

## Challenging UK market [...] The second largest, LloydsPharmacy, has divested more than 200 pharmacies since 2016, and the fourth largest, Rowlands Pharmacy, announced in February 2019 that it plans to sell 70 of its branches.

The fact that large multiples, which make up 49.4% of the market and include companies with 100 or more pharmacies (see Infographic), are feeling the squeeze is perhaps not surprising. Like small multiples (companies with between six and 99 pharmacies) and independents, they have endured several financial challenges over the past few years.

> The current funding climate is holding back community pharmacy from its huge potential to improve outcomes for patients and reduce the pressures on GPs and [accident and emergency] departments

Budget headlines

Rachel Reeves’ first Budget was dominated by the headline figure of £40bn worth of tax rises. The changes, which are scheduled to take effect from April 6, include an increase in employer National Insurance (NI) contributions from 13.8 per cent on salaries over £9,100 to 15 per cent on salaries above £5,000.

The NI tax rise does not apply to the NHS, but this exemption has not yet been confirmed for other primary care providers, including community pharmacies, GP practices and care homes. In 2025, it is vital that pharmacies receive the right support to allow them to successfully navigate this new financial landscape. This could be achieved by strengthening government guarantee schemes to help improve SME access to finance and ensure they can manage increased costs. [...] In Scotland, changes to the Government-set tariff mechanism helped to alleviate some of the pressures. In September, Community Pharmacy Scotland (CPS) confirmed it had secured a 6 per cent funding uplift for the sector in a “long-awaited” 2024-25 funding package. CPS accepted the Scottish Government’s offer of a deal, with the guaranteed minimum for Drug Tariff reimbursement set at £110m – £10m higher than in 2023-24.

However, this positive step forward was curtailed by the delivery of Labour’s Westminster autumn Budget just one month later, which brought some expected announcements as well as a few surprises.

Budget headlines [...] Community pharmacies are key contributors to the UK economy, as well as being frontline providers of primary care. The upheaval of 2024 demonstrated that the sector is robust and responsive to change. As we enter 2025, it is vital that pharmacy owners receive the clarity and support they need to deliver their ambition – for the greater benefit of patients, communities and staff.

## Shift in ownership patterns

The data also reveals a notable shift in ownership dynamics across the sector.

Small independent pharmacy owners—defined as those operating between one and five pharmacies—now hold the largest market share at over 49 per cent.

Their numbers have grown significantly from 4,024 in 2021 to 4,910 in March 2025, an increase of 886.

Medium-sized groups (owning 6 to 99 pharmacies) now account for over 18 per cent of the market, with 1,807 pharmacies recorded as of March 2025.

In contrast, large pharmacy chains (owning 100 or more pharmacies) have seen a steep decline. Their numbers have plummeted from 5,220 in 2021 to just 3,283—a reduction of 1,938.

They now represent only 32.8 per cent of the total market. [...] See Full Bio

The total number of bricks-and-mortar community pharmacies in England has dropped below 10,000, according to the latest data from the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA).

As of the end of March 2025, there were 9,999 community pharmacies (excluding distance selling pharmacies) operating in England—down from 10,837 at the beginning of 2021. This marks a net loss of 838 pharmacies over four years.

Between January 2024 and March 2025 alone, England recorded 274 pharmacy closures, averaging more than five closures per week.

When including distance selling pharmacies, the total number of pharmacies in England now stands at 10,407, down from 11,206 in January 2021.

# Almost five million Pharmacy First consultations delivered in first year

A man and an older lady stand at a pharmacy counter 

SolStock / E+ via Getty Images

Almost five million Pharmacy First consultations were delivered in the first year of the service in England, official data has confirmed.

The latest data from the NHS Business Services Authority (NHSBSA) shows that contractors in England submitted claims for 4,941,308 Pharmacy First consultations between February 2024 and January 2025.

Of those, more than half (2,735,577) were referred into pharmacies from GP surgeries or NHS111 and were claimed as minor illness or urgent medicine supply referrals. [...] In January 2025, contractors had to complete 25 clinical pathway consultations to be eligible for the £1,000 monthly payment – an increase from the 20 required in December.

The increase meant that fewer contractors were able to meet the threshold, and just 4,940 contractors were eligible for the monthly payment in January – down from 6,194 the month before.

Overall, 9,265, or 87% of contractors in England, delivered at least one Pharmacy First consultation in January 2025, suggesting that the service is active in almost nine in ten pharmacies.

Tase Oputu, chair of the England board of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society (RPS), said the figures ‘show the real impact Pharmacy First is having, with millions of patients getting faster access to care and easing pressure on GPs.’ [...] He said the service was ‘an important stepping stone towards a more clinical future’, and CPE was advocating for the service to include more clinical pathways and independent prescribing in the future.

Total numbers of both clinical pathway and referral consultations dropped slightly in January 2025 after reaching their highest levels yet in December 2024.

Nick Thayer, head of policy, told The Pharmacist that it was ‘common to see spikes of Pharmacy First consultations around bank holidays and when other providers may not be readily accessible’.

And he cited analysis of CCA pharmacies that found a 15% increase in activity during the CrowdStrike IT outage in July 2024 and a 10% increase in activity in the week leading up to Christmas.

The announcement represents an important recognition of the vital role community pharmacies play in improving access to care, supporting patients closer to home and relieving pressure on other parts of the healthcare system. Pharmacists who hold an independent prescribing qualification will be able to assess patients and prescribe medicines directly, building on the success of the Pharmacy First service. The changes, which will be rolled out from autumn 2026, will reduce the number of referrals back to GPs, boosting efficiency and improving both patient experience and outcomes [...] 1. A Relentless "Squeeze" from Inflation and Wages
The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) notes that an 8.9% budget increase was required in 2026 simply for pharmacies to "stand still" against soaring operational costs.
The new 10.3% framework barely clears that threshold.
Pharmacies must fully absorb massive overhead hikes, including surging National Living Wage costs, heightened business rates, and volatile utility bills.
2. Doing More Work for Less Core Funding
While a £3.64 billion total funding pot is locked in for the year, the actual fee paid to pharmacies for dispensing medicine (the Single Activity Fee) only increased by a minimal 6p to £1.52 per item. [...] 📢 Community Pharmacy Funding: Progress, but the work is far from over.
Community Pharmacy England (CPE) has secured a 10.3% funding increase for community pharmacies in 2026/27, taking total funding to £3.636 billion. The settlement also includes a £200 million uplift to retained margin, a write-off of up to £239 million in margin recovery, and the planned introduction of Independent Prescribing services later this year.
These developments represent an important recognition of the value that community pharmacies bring to patients, local communities, and the wider NHS. At a time when pharmacies continue to face rising operational costs, increasing patient demand, workforce pressures, and medicine supply challenges, any investment in the sector is welcome.

The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) has advised its 6,000 member pharmacies in England to limit pharmacy services from 1 April 2025 “if no new and sufficient funding is delivered”.

In a statement published on 18 March 2025, the NPA said the action was being taken “to protect patients, in the absence of a financial settlement that covers a swathe of new costs due to hit pharmacies from the start of next month”.

It added that these costs include increases in national insurance, national living wage and business rates, “on top of a decade of real-terms cuts, which may jeopardise patient safety if a resolution is not found”. [...] The NPA first proposed collective action in September 2024, when it balloted members over limiting services in protest against pharmacy funding levels.

In response to the ballot, 98% of pharmacy owners in England voted in favour of the action.

The collective action could include closing outside minimum contract hours, withdrawing from locally commissioned services, providing free home deliveries and refusing to cooperate with some data requests.

In January 2025, the government announced that it had started negotiations with Community Pharmacy England (CPE) on the ‘Community pharmacy contractual framework’ for 2024/2025 and 2025/2026. [...] Skip to content

### Community pharmacy real terms funding reduction

2. Throughout the inquiry, we heard about the financial pressures on community pharmacy. Research commissioned by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) found that one in three English community pharmacies were operating in deficit in 2020.1 By 2022 funding levels had dropped by over 30% in real terms since 2015, with the proportion of total NHS funding used to meet community pharmacy service costs reducing from circa 2.4% to 1.6% in under a decade.2 [...] 5. We also heard about the possible impact of not addressing these funding challenges. The CCA’s February 2024 analysis of NHS data shows that there are now over 1,110 fewer pharmacies in England since 2015. There has been a net loss of almost 400 community pharmacies in England since the start of the 2023/24 financial year. Between 2015 and February 2024, 34.9% of closures occurred in the 20% most deprived neighbourhoods in the country.6 Jay Badenhorst, then Vice Chair of the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) warned:

If the network is not sustained and appropriately funded, and at some point that network is not there any longer, we are not going to get it back. Once it has gone, our invaluable asset doing very good public services will be gone.7 [...] 71. But there have been challenges around the delivery of the service. The Pharmacists’ Defence Association (PDA), which represents pharmacists, told us of their “significant concerns about the timescales and methods of implementation” of Pharmacy First. The PDA conducted research amongst its members and “98% of respondents reported that they have insufficient staffing to operate existing community pharmacy services”. The research also found concern about “competence and confidence” and the PDA told us that “it has been impossible for some pharmacists to complete training for any gaps in clinical knowledge highlighted as part of a competency self-assessment due to course availability or an absence of protected learning time”.97
